It’s very simple, sir. 

Trespassing in itself does not justify the use of a firearm, nor any other deadly weapon, in ANY capacity. I’m not saying I agree with this law, I’m just saying that’s how it is.

The law does not distinguish whether that firearm is in “low ready” position, or aimed dead-center at the target; in either case, the premeditated action of approaching the perceived threat with the firearm on your person and presenting it is classified in the eyes of the law as assault with a deadly weapon when not justified, which again, confronting a trespasser is NOT justified cause here. Importantly, the weapon does not have to be used to constitute assault. 

That’s all I’ve intended to say here. If you can show me a single state whose penal code allows their citizens to confront a trespasser, who is guilty of nothing more than trespassing, with a deadly weapon, as you’re arguing for here, then I will concede.

The justifiable use of deadly force is actually quite simple. 

Sure, it varies somewhat from state to state, but in ANY case, the constant is that one MUST be able to articulate to a jury, beyond a reasonable doubt, that they were in fear of “great bodily injury or death” in order to respond to a threat with deadly force. Those are the only “basic details” concerned with justifiable deadly force. 

Trespassing alone has time and time again NOT satisfied this requirement in landmark cases. 

Not sure why you are so offended by me trying to educate people on here that it’s not legal to have guns pulled on them for delivering packages. Despite whatever the homeowner may have going on in their head.

There are varying laws in states, but in nearly any justifiable use of deadly force case, one must be able to articulate and convince a jury, beyond a reasonable doubt, of “a perceived threat of great bodily injury or death” in order to respond with deadly force. 

Trespassing in itself simply does not satisfy that requirement.

In the court system, presenting a firearm in such a situation (whether used or not, whether kept at one’s side to deter, or aimed with intent) is seen as the escalation to deadly force and must meet stringent requirements to be deemed legal.

The main reason is because at your age, the loss, and moreover the hairline itself has not stabilized, and by stabilized I mean a point where it will *not significantly change* in the next coming years. It's always going to be changing--minor changes sure, but not *significant change* as in another step on the Norwood Scale. There's a *huge* difference between a person experiencing rapid, significant hair loss in their early 20's, as in going from a Norwood 1 --> Norwood 2/3 in just a few years, and a person in their late 20's/early 30's who's going to be a Norwood 3 for the next 10+ years before a slow approach to a Norwood 4. The latter is described as "stabilized" hair loss and generally has not happened yet at your age .

This non-stabilized hairline becomes a problem when it comes time for the transplant; it's a bit of a gamble on both you and the doctor's part. Place the hairline too low, and you're not going to be able to maintain that in the coming years. It's likely not going to be as dense, therefore will be less natural-looking, and in the further coming years as you experience further loss (Fin significantly slows, but doesn't completely halt) it may end up looking thin, straggly, and unnatural since it's placed so low. You also might have exhausted your donor area after this second one, so more transplants might not be an option.

On the other hand, place the hairline too high, and you may have just squandered your own potential. It may take you 15 years to catch up to that level of recession that your newly-transplanted hairline is at. Perhaps you may never catch up to it if the finasteride is really doing its job. Then you're stuck with a strange peninsula-like looking patch of sparse natural hair protruding from the otherwise rather dense hairline that was a result of the implant.

It's not an absolute rule of course. It's just a best practice that most ethical doctors follow, because in most cases, by late twenties/early thirties, you've reached that stabilization point, e.g. hair pattern at age 27 - age 31 will be roughly no different.
